newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees continued commercial aviation growth.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees continued commercial aviation growth.

text.p: U.S. airlines carried 605 million passengers in 1996 and can be expected to fly more this year and nearly one billion by the year 2008, the Federal Aviation Administration said Wednesday.

In its annual aviation forecast, the FAA said passenger traffic on domestic routes flown by the large U.S. carriers would increase by 4.3 percent, to 546 million, and would post an average annual rise of 3.9 percent through 2008.
Their international traffic would rise by about 5.5 percent this year, to 53 million, and post an average of 5.8 percent a year through 2008, it said.
The agency said that Pacific traffic would again lead the growth, by 6.5 percent a year over the next 10 years, and Latin American traffic would rise by 6.3 percent.

Overall foreign passengers flown by U.S. and foreign lines were forecast to rise by 5.9 percent this year, to 100.4 million, and by 5.7 percent a year over the next 12 years, to 183.6 million, the agency said.
The forecasts followed rises recorded in 1996 over 1995.
Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater said the increase of the past year and future gains come against the industry's third straight year of strong growth.
For 1996, the FAA said, the commercial aviation industry reported an operating profit of $6 billion, a $700 million increase over the previous year.

Slater said that new FAA air traffic technologies, tougher oversight and maintenance and a single level of safety for both big jets and small commuter planes should enable the FAA to meet the future needs of the growing U.S. aviation system.
The FAA predicted the U.S. jet fleet would increase from its 4,775 aircraft last year to 7,226 in 2008, an annual increase of 3.5 percent.
Commuter traffic was also forecast to increase, to 62.5 million this year or up 8.7 percent, to an average increase of 5.3 percent annually, to 107 million in 2008.
The FAA added that the commuter fleet would rise from 2,090 planes in 1996 to 2,909 at the end of the forecast period.
